title: Farm Business Management and Farming Process Management

lessons.title: The fruit farm as a business
lessons.html:
The fruit farm as a business

A fruit or wine grape farm is a business that must make a profit to survive, pay workers and reinvest in blocks and equipment. A foreman who understands the business side makes better daily decisions.

The value chain

Fruit moves from the orchard to the packhouse, through cold storage and shipping to export markets or to local markets, retailers and processors. Wine grapes go to a cellar. At each step costs are added and the farm's share of the final price depends on quality, timing and volume. Export fruit is often sold through export agents, and the farm is paid after the fruit is sold, sometimes months after harvest.

Income and costs

Income comes from the cartons or tonnes sold, at prices that depend on market, size, grade and season. Costs include:

  • Direct (variable) costs: labour, fertiliser, chemicals, fuel, packaging, picking costs - these rise with production.
  • Overhead (fixed) costs: management salaries, insurance, rates, loan interest, depreciation of machinery and blocks.

Gross margin is income minus direct costs for a block or crop. It shows which blocks contribute most to covering overheads and profit.

Yield and quality drive income

Packout percentage - the share of harvested fruit that makes export grade - is as important as tonnes per hectare. A block with high yield but poor packout because of blemishes or small size may earn less than a block with lower yield and excellent packout. Many foreman decisions - thinning, spraying, picking care - directly affect packout.

Labour cost

Labour is usually the largest direct cost on fruit farms. Productive, well-organised teams and low absenteeism make a big difference to profit.

lessons.title: Budgets, cost control and records
lessons.html:
Budgets, cost control and records

The budget

The farm manager prepares an annual budget per block or crop: expected yield, income, and costs for each operation (pruning, thinning, spraying, fertilising, irrigation, harvest). The foreman's operations must be carried out within this budget.

Cost per operation

For each job, the main costs are labour hours, materials and machine hours. A simple example for hand thinning a block:

ItemCalculation
LabourWorkers x hours x hourly rate
SupervisionForeman hours x rate
TransportTractor or bakkie hours x cost per hour
Cost per hectareTotal / hectares

Comparing actual cost per hectare with the budget and with previous seasons shows where efficiency can improve.

Controlling costs

  • Plan work to avoid idle time, double handling and waiting for equipment.
  • Use materials at the recommended rates; calibrate sprayers and spreaders.
  • Do jobs at the right time - late shoot thinning or late spraying costs more and achieves less.
  • Prevent waste and losses: tools, fuel, chemicals.
  • Report overspending early with reasons.

Records

Good records are the base of cost control and also of market access. Export food safety and sustainability audits (such as GLOBALG.A.P. and local schemes) require records of sprays, fertiliser, irrigation, worker training, hygiene and traceability. Daily job cards per block - who worked, how many hours, what was done, materials used - feed both the cost system and the audit file.

Capital decisions

Decisions such as replanting a block, installing netting or buying a new sprayer are investments evaluated over many years. The foreman's records on block performance and machinery condition support these decisions.

lessons.title: Managing the farming process
lessons.html:
Managing the farming process

The production calendar

Fruit production follows a strict seasonal sequence: winter pruning and dormant sprays, bud break, flowering and pollination, thinning, canopy work, fruit growth, harvest and post-harvest care. Each operation has a window. The foreman uses the calendar to plan labour, equipment and materials weeks ahead.

Plan - do - check - act

  1. Plan: list operations per block for the coming weeks, with standards, labour, equipment and materials.
  2. Do: brief teams, allocate work, and supervise.
  3. Check: inspect quality, measure progress against plan, check costs.
  4. Act: correct problems and improve the plan for next time.

Priorities

When resources are short, prioritise operations that protect the crop and have hard deadlines, such as disease sprays before rain, frost protection or harvest of ripe fruit, over jobs that can wait a few days, such as mowing.

Risk management

RiskExample responses
Hail, frost, windNetting, frost protection, windbreaks, insurance
Pest or disease outbreakScouting, timely sprays, IPM
Labour shortages at harvestEarly recruitment, training, retention
Water shortageScheduling, maintenance, storage, legal allocation
Market rejectionQuality control, residue compliance, traceability

Communication with management

Report progress, problems and costs regularly and in writing. Raise risks early with suggested solutions. Managers rely on the foreman's information from the blocks to make business decisions.

Key points

  • Profit depends on yield, packout, price and cost control.
  • Gross margin is income minus direct costs for a block.
  • Labour is usually the largest direct cost.
  • Track actual cost per operation against budget.
  • Use plan-do-check-act and prioritise crop-protecting, deadline tasks.
